traveler: Rabbi Benjamin son of Jonah of Tudela (Benjamin de Tudela)
title: The Book of Travels: a Navarrese Rabbi Counts the Jews of the World, Tudela to Baghdad and Home
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tudela, the setting out
stops.date_confidence: Unfixed. Adler's editions differ between 1159 and 1165; the Jewish Encyclopedia keeps the traditional 1160; modern consensus favours c. 1165, and Adler's footnote 2 brackets his absence from Europe between 1166 and 1171. The month and day are defaults, not evidence.
stops.campa: Benjamin son of Jonah leaves the town on the Ebro where he was born, in the kingdom of Navarre, and the book he brings back opens with that fact and nothing else: no age, no trade, no household named, no reason given. Four centuries earlier Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi mustered his host at Pamplona in this same kingdom and rode north to a field he did not return from. Benjamin rides east, alone in the text, counting. He will name some two hundred and forty-eight community leaders between here and the Tigris, and not one word about himself.
suggested_refs: The opening lines of the Sefer ha-Masa'ot, naming Tudela as the native city and the point of departure
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), p. 1, Project Gutenberg 14981-h
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Benjamin of Tudela'

stops.name: Zaragoza, the first stage
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the departure year; Adler gives no interval at all for the Tudela to Saragossa leg, so the stage cannot be dated on its own.
stops.campa: He crosses out of Navarre at once. Saragossa lies in Aragon, one frontier from home, and the Itinerary gives no interval for the stage: I journeyed first from my native town to the city of Saragossa, and that is all. From here the road runs down the Ebro to Tortosa, then Tarragona of the cyclopean Greek stonework, then the coast. The method of the whole book is already fixed on its first page. A town, a number of Jews, the names of the men who lead them, the distance to the next town, and no traveller visible anywhere in it.
suggested_refs: The Ebro road from Tudela through Saragossa to Tortosa, first stages of the Itinerary
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Barcelona, the Call by the sea
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Adler gives two days from Tarragona; the absolute year rests on the departure date, which is itself unfixed.
stops.campa: The Call sits inside the walls of a small city on the sea, and Benjamin writes it down as he writes every other: R. Shesheth, R. Shealtiel, R. Solomon, R. Abraham son of Chisdai. Merchants come thither from all quarters, he says, from Greece and Pisa and Genoa and Alexandria and the land of Israel. A century and a quarter later Ramon Llull will take a royal licence in this city to preach inside the synagogues of the Crown of Aragon. Benjamin does not preach. He counts, and he is gone within the week.
suggested_refs: The Call of medieval Barcelona; the identification of Benjamin's R. Shesheth with Sheshet ben Isaac Benveniste is a modern inference, not in the text
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
ramon_llull.journey.json

stops.name: Narbonne, whence the Law goes forth
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the route order and the departure year; no date is given in the text.
stops.campa: Three hundred Jews, and at their head R. Kalonymos son of R. Todros, who holds land from the lords of the town and traces his line to the House of David. Benjamin has crossed into a country where Jewish learning is not merely tolerated but exported, and he says so in one clause that will be quoted for eight hundred years. He lists the sages by name, as though a census of scholars were the same act as a census of souls. In his book it is. From Narbonne the road runs on through Beziers, Montpellier and Lunel, each with its own number.
stops.quote: thence the Torah (Law) goes forth to all countries. Sages, and great and illustrious men abide here.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Narbonne
suggested_refs: The Narbonne nesi'im and the tradition of Davidic descent among the Kalonymos family
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Lunel, the students boarded and clothed
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order; the text gives distances in days, never a calendar date.
stops.campa: About three hundred Jews, and among them R. Judah ibn Tibbon, the Physician, the Sephardi, who is turning the Arabic philosophy of Andalusia into Hebrew for men who can no longer read it. The house of study is headed by Rabbenu Meshullam and his five sons. What Benjamin records at Lunel is not a doctrine but an arrangement: the congregation feeds, houses, clothes and teaches any student who comes from a distant land, for as long as he stays at the books. He is himself a man from a distant land, passing through.
stops.quote: The students that come from distant lands to learn the Law are taught, boarded, lodged and clothed by the congregation, so long as they attend the house of study.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Lunel
suggested_refs: The yeshiva of Lunel under Meshullam ben Jacob; the Tibbonid workshop of Hebrew translation
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Marseille, the upper and the lower congregation
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The sailing season is inferred from the four-day crossing to Genoa the text records, not from any statement of date.
stops.campa: Two congregations, upper and lower, about three hundred souls between them, each with its own scholars, and the ships. Benjamin has walked the length of Provence and now stops walking. Four days out from this harbour lies Genoa. He goes aboard, and the book changes character with him: from here the stages are counted in days at sea, and the towns arrive out of the water one after another, each with its number of Jews already waiting to be written down. Nothing is said about weather, seasickness, fear, or the price of passage.
suggested_refs: The two congregations of twelfth-century Marseille and the Provencal shipping season
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Genoa, the city of consuls
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed; Adler gives four days at sea from Marseille and no year.
stops.campa: A city surrounded by a wall, subject to no king, governed by judges whom the citizens appoint at their own pleasure. Its galleys go out to plunder and to trade as far as Sicily and the coast of Africa, and its houses have towers, and when the towers quarrel the men fight from the roofs. In all of it Benjamin finds two Jews, brothers, R. Samuel son of Salim and his brother, come from Ceuta. He writes both names down. Damascus, when he reaches it, will get three thousand souls and one rabbi's name, and no more room on the page than this.
suggested_refs: The consular republic of Genoa and its tower-houses in the twelfth century
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Rome, the steward in the Pope's house
stops.date_confidence: The one European anchor Adler accepts: footnote 2 places Benjamin in Rome between late 1165 and 1167. Month and day are defaults. Note the pin marks the Portico d'Ottavia, site of the 1555 ghetto; Benjamin's community lived across the river in Trastevere.
stops.campa: Two hundred Jews across the river in Trastevere, paying no tribute, and one of them keeps the keys of the papal household. R. Jechiel, a young man, grandson of the R. Nathan who compiled the Arukh, is steward of everything Pope Alexander owns. Benjamin walks the ruins with an inventory in hand: the palace of Titus, the eighty halls of Vespasian, the cave where Titus son of Vespasian hid, the pillars of Samson, and in the church of St. John in the Lateran the two bronze columns carried out of the Temple at Jerusalem.
stops.quote: Rome is the head of the kingdoms of Christendom, and contains about 200 Jews, who occupy an honourable position and pay no tribute, and amongst them are officials of the Pope Alexander, the spiritual head of all Christendom.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Rome
suggested_refs: The Trastevere Jewish quarter of twelfth-century Rome; the bronze Temple columns Benjamin reports at the Lateran
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h, and n. 2
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Rome'

stops.name: Salerno, six hundred beside the medical school
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order between the Rome anchor and the Byzantine crossing.
stops.campa: Six hundred Jews in the city of the Christian physicians, where medicine is taught as a science with a school and a syllabus, the first such place in Latin Europe. Benjamin names the rabbis, not the doctors. He is running down the Italian leg at speed now: Capua three hundred, Naples five hundred, Amalfi twenty whose men live by trade and not by the plough, Benevento two hundred, Melfi two hundred, Trani two hundred where the pilgrims of all nations take ship for Jerusalem, Taranto three hundred, Brindisi ten dyers.
stops.quote: R. Judah, son of R. Isaac, the son of Melchizedek, the great Rabbi, who came from the city of Siponto
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Salerno
suggested_refs: The Schola Medica Salernitana and the Jewish communities of the Norman south
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Otranto, the crossing to the Greek sea
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Note a contradiction inside the research pool: one lens gives Otranto 500 Jews, another 50. Adler reads 'about 50 Jews'.
stops.campa: Fifty Jews on the coast of the Greek sea, and the last Latin ground under him before the crossing. Two days out lies Corfu. Benjamin has come down from Trani, where the pilgrims of every nation embark for Jerusalem, and at Otranto he takes the shorter water, the one that leads not to the Holy Land but to the empire of the Greeks. He will reach Jerusalem eventually, by the long way round, through Constantinople and the islands and the whole coast of the Franks, and it will take him more than a year to arrive at it.
suggested_refs: The Otranto to Corfu crossing, the standard Apulian passage into Byzantine waters
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Corfu, one Jew named Joseph
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order; two days from Otranto by the text, no year given.
stops.campa: One Jew lives on Corfu, and his name is R. Joseph. Benjamin gives him a line to himself, the same line he would give a city, and adds the sentence that closes a kingdom: here ends the kingdom of Sicily. The Greek dominion does not begin at the island. It begins one stage further on, in the land of Larta, which is the beginning of the dominions of Emanuel, Sovereign of the Greeks. Between the two lies a strip of water with a single man in it, counted, and the entry ends there.
suggested_refs: The Sicilian-Byzantine frontier of 1166, which the text places between Corfu and Arta, not at Corfu
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Thebes, the silk and the purple
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order through Arta, Patras, Corinth; the text counts days between towns and never years.
stops.campa: Two thousand Jews, the largest community he finds in all of Greece, and the looms that dress the emperor. Purple here is not a colour but a monopoly, and the men who know the murex and the mordants are Jews, and Manuel Komnenos needs them. Benjamin names their scholars, R. Aaron, R. Moses, R. Hiyya, R. Elijah Tirutot, R. Joktan, and says there are none like them in the land of the Greeks except at Constantinople. A Sicilian fleet will carry the weavers of Thebes off to Palermo within a generation of his passing.
stops.quote: Thence it is two days' journey to the great city of Thebes, where there are about 2,000 Jews. They are the most skilled artificers in silk and purple cloth throughout Greece.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Thebes
suggested_refs: The Theban silk workshops and the imperial purple monopoly under Manuel I Komnenos
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Constantinople, the quarter behind the inlet
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Adler's bracket for the absence from Europe (1166-1171) contains it; the research pool's chronology lens dates the Constantinople stop 1167. The year is not fixed by any statement in the text.
stops.campa: The greatest city of the world lies open in front of him and he is not allowed to sleep in it. The Jewish quarter is at Pera, across the Golden Horn, reached by boat, and the tanneries are set among the houses so that the streets stink and the Greeks say so aloud. The emperor Manuel keeps a palace on the shore covered over with gold and silver, and takes twenty thousand gold pieces a year in tribute from the merchants of every nation, and no Jew in his empire may ride a horse. There is one exception.
stops.quote: No Jews live in the city, for they have been placed behind an inlet of the sea.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Constantinople
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Pera across the Golden Horn and the tanners' district of twelfth-century Constantinople
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Constantinople, the fence and the physician
stops.date_confidence: Same visit as the preceding stop, split for what it records; the date is a placement, not evidence.
stops.campa: The exception is R. Solomon Hamitsri, physician to the emperor, and through him the community buys what relief it can. Benjamin counts twenty-five hundred Jews in the quarter and then does what no Christian traveller in Constantinople does: he counts the fence. Rabbanites on one side, Karaites on the other, a partition between two readings of one Law, both under the same Greek contempt. He gives the partition one clause, takes ship for Rhaedestus and Gallipoli and the islands, and keeps counting.
stops.quote: In the Jewish quarter are about 2,000 Rabbanite Jews and about 500 Karaites, and a fence divides them.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Constantinople
suggested_refs: The Rabbanite and Karaite congregations of Pera, separated by a physical partition
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Cyprus, the sect that waits for morning
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed, and the pin is a placement: Benjamin names no port or city on Cyprus. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from ramon_llull.journey.json (Famagusta) so the two travellers share one Cypriot point.
stops.campa: Rhodes behind him, then Cyprus, where there are Rabbanite Jews and Karaites and a third sort, whom he calls Epikursin and whom the others excommunicate in every place. They keep the Sabbath from the morning of the seventh day and profane the eve of it. Benjamin fixes no harbour, no city, no host; the island enters the book as a doctrine and a coastline. Ramon Llull will land at Famagusta in 1301 with a plan for converting the Latin East, and find the same island a way station toward somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The Cypriot Epikursin, a sect known only from this passage of the Itinerary
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
ramon_llull.journey.json

stops.name: Tripoli, the earthquake and the Sheik al Hashishim
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The earthquakes he reports are conventionally dated 1157, a decade before his passage; he records them as recent, not as witnessed.
stops.campa: The Sheik al Hashishim holds eight days' journey of mountain from the fortress of Kadmus, and his people obey him to the death, and the Franks and the ruler of Tripoli both go in fear of him. Benjamin passes below that country on the coast road. Tripoli itself he enters under a death toll: an earthquake threw the city down and more than twenty thousand died, and at Hamah the same shaking killed twenty-five thousand, of whom a hundred and thirty were Jews and seventy of those came out alive.
suggested_refs: The Nizari Ismaili territory around Qadmus; the 1157 Syrian earthquake sequence at Tripoli and Hamah
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Tyre, the harbour closed with chains
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order. The research pool's two lenses give Tyre 400 and 500 Jews; Adler reads 500.
stops.campa: Five hundred Jews, some of them scholars of the Talmud, and a harbour a man can shut. Iron chains run from tower to tower across the mouth at nightfall, and nothing goes in or out until morning. Tyre makes sugar and it makes glass, and the glass carries the city's name into every country that buys it. Benjamin looks down from the walls into the water and reports the ruins of the old Tyre lying under the sea, streets and towers still visible to anyone who sails across them on a clear day.
stops.quote: The Jews own sea-going vessels, and there are glass-makers amongst them who make that fine Tyrian glass-ware which is prized in all countries.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Tyre
suggested_refs: The chained harbour of Crusader Tyre and its Jewish glass and sugar industries
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Acre, where the pilgrims land
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from richard_lionheart.journey.json.
stops.campa: Two hundred Jews, and the gate of the whole business: Acre is where the pilgrim ships put down the Christians of every nation bound for Jerusalem, and where Benjamin steps onto the soil of Israel. It is the commencement of the land, he writes, and it stands upon the Great Sea. Richard of England will take this port by siege in July 1191, a quarter of a century after Benjamin walks off the quay, and Marco Polo will sail out of it eastward in 1271, past the same towers and the same harbour mole.
suggested_refs: The pilgrim harbour of Crusader Acre, landfall for the Jerusalem road
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Mount Carmel, the cave of Elijah
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed; the day is a placement within the coastal leg, not a recorded date.
stops.campa: Under the mountain lies Haifa, which is Hahepher on the seaboard, and above it the cave of Elijah, over which the Christians have built a house and named it St. Elias. At the foot runs the brook Kishon, where the prophets of Baal were killed. Jewish sepulchres are cut into the rock nearby. Benjamin, who has been counting living Jews for two years, begins here to count dead ones as well: the graves become stations, and the book turns from a census into a pilgrimage without altering its voice by a syllable.
suggested_refs: Elijah's Cave on Mount Carmel and the Christian structure of St. Elias reported over it
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Jerusalem, under the Tower of David
stops.date_confidence: Contested, and not resolved here. The research pool's two lenses date the Jerusalem visit c. 1169 and 1170; both postdate the Raqqa synchronism (no later than 26 October 1168), which the Itinerary's own route order places after Jerusalem. No arrangement satisfies all three. This placement follows route order and the Raqqa anchor.
stops.campa: The city is small, strongly walled, and full of Jacobites, Syrians, Greeks, Georgians and Franks, and pilgrims of every tongue. The Jews of it live in one corner beneath the Tower of David, holding by lease from the king the sole right to dye cloth in Jerusalem. Two hundred souls hold the monopoly, and the citadel wall stands at their backs. A variant manuscript reading gives the number of dyers as four rather than the full two hundred souls of the quarter, a discrepancy the critical text does not resolve.
stops.quote: There are about 200 Jews who dwell under the Tower of David in one corner of the city.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Jerusalem
suggested_refs: The Tower of David quarter of Crusader Jerusalem; note that the widely quoted 'about four Jewish dyers' is a variant manuscript reading, not Adler's critical text
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Jerusalem, the sanctuary held by the Franks
stops.date_confidence: Same visit as the preceding stop. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from ibn_battuta.journey.json, the atlas's canonical Temple Mount pin, which maimonides.journey.json also sits beside.
stops.campa: On the platform stand two houses of the orders: the hospital, where four hundred knights take in the sick, and the Templum Domini, which was the Temple of Solomon, where three hundred knights are quartered and ride out to war. Omar ben al Khataab built a great dome over the rock, and no image is set up inside it. Crusader tradition identified the dome with Solomon's own Temple, a conflation of the Islamic shrine with the Jewish site it replaced that the military orders inherited along with the ground itself.
stops.quote: It contains a dyeing-house, for which the Jews pay a small rent annually to the king, on condition that besides the Jews no other dyers be allowed in Jerusalem.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Jerusalem
suggested_refs: The Templum Domini and the Hospital of St. John as Benjamin describes them; the Dome of the Rock reported as a place of prayer without images
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
maimonides.journey.json
ibn_battuta.journey.json

stops.name: Bethlehem, the pillar of eleven stones
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed; the text gives two parasangs from Jerusalem and no date.
stops.campa: Two parasangs out of Jerusalem, twelve Jews dyeing cloth, and half a mile beyond the town the grave of Rachel on the road. The pillar over it is built of eleven stones, one for each of the sons Jacob had while she lived, and the twelfth son was the birth that killed her, and his name was Benjamin. The traveller writing this down carries that name. He does not remark on it. He gives the stones their number, notes that Jews who pass cut their own names into them, and goes on to Hebron.
suggested_refs: Rachel's tomb on the Bethlehem road and its eleven-stone pillar, counted for the sons born before Benjamin
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Hebron, the descent beneath St Abraham
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order. Coordinate corrected: two entries in the research pool pin Machpelah about a kilometre off, at 31.5256, 35.1004 and 31.5326, 35.0998.
stops.campa: The old city on the mountain is waste; the town stands now in the valley, and the Christians have built a church over the field of Machpelah and call it St. Abraham. A Jew who comes with a fee is taken by the keepers through an iron gate and down into three caves, the first empty, the second empty, and then the third, where six sepulchres face one another with the names of the patriarchs and their wives cut into them in Hebrew. A lamp burns there day and night. Benjamin pays, descends, and writes down what he is shown.
suggested_refs: The Cave of Machpelah under the Crusader church of St. Abraham, and the fee charged to Jewish visitors
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
The Jewish Community of Hebron, 'Benjamin of Tudela Describes the Tomb of Machpela'

stops.name: Damascus, three thousand and the crystal wall
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The research pool's chronology lens dates the Damascus notice 1167 but the Itinerary's route order places it after the Judaean stops. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from bernard_clairvaux.journey.json.
stops.campa: Three thousand Jews under an academy headed by R. Azariah, and beside them a hundred Karaites and four hundred Samaritans, who live at peace with one another and do not intermarry. The city is walled about with gardens and orchards fed by the Amana, and in the great mosque hangs a wall of glass in which a man can find his own house among all the houses of Damascus. Benjamin walks the length of that wall before he ever reaches the academy, counting houses in the glass the way he is about to count souls in the register, one habit feeding the other, and he walks in at the gate and counts.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque and its reported glass wall; the Rabbanite, Karaite and Samaritan communities of Nurid Damascus
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Tadmor, two thousand who take spoil
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from route order; the text gives days from Baalbek and no year.
stops.campa: Tadmor in the desert, which Solomon built of the same enormous stones as Baalbek, and two thousand Jews in it who are men of war. They fight in the quarrels of their Arab neighbours and against the Christians of Edom, and they take their share of what is taken. Benjamin has been counting communities that survive by being useful to a king: by dyeing, by glass, by silk, by medicine. Here he writes one that survives by fighting, and gives it the same flat two clauses he gave the weavers of Thebes.
suggested_refs: Palmyra and its armed Jewish community as reported in the Itinerary
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Aleppo, Aram Zoba
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The research pool dates the Aleppo notice 1168; the placement here follows route order between Damascus and the Raqqa anchor.
stops.campa: Aram Zoba, which is Aleppo, the royal city of King Nur al-Din, standing in a country with no spring and no river, where every household keeps a cistern and the rain is the whole water supply. Five thousand Jews, and R. Moses el-Constantini and R. Seth at their head. Benjamin is now inside the power that faces the Franks he has just left, and the book does not change tone across the frontier. From Aleppo the road bends east toward the Euphrates and the country of the Head of the Captivity.
suggested_refs: Aleppo as Nur al-Din's royal city and the cistern water supply Benjamin describes
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Raqqa, the anchor in the year
stops.date_confidence: The firmest anchor on the whole road, and still [R]: no earlier than late summer 1167, when Nur al-Din ceded the city to his youngest brother, and no later than 26 October 1168. It reaches this file through a search summary of the article literature, not the articles themselves.
stops.campa: On the Euphrates, at the edge of the desert that divides Shinar from the land of Aram, about seven hundred Jews, and the synagogue built by Ezra the Scribe when he went up out of Babylon to Jerusalem. Raqqa is the one place on the entire road that pins Benjamin to a calendar. Nur al-Din hands the city to his youngest brother in the late summer of 1167, and Benjamin describes the arrangement as it stands; a documented change closes the window on the twenty-sixth of October 1168. Everything else is inferred from it.
suggested_refs: The Raqqa synchronism used by modern scholars to date the eastward leg of the Itinerary
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
search summary of the scholarship on the Itinerary's dating (article literature not consulted directly)

stops.name: Mosul, Assur the Great
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the Raqqa window and route order; the pool dates the Mosul notice 1168.
stops.campa: Assur the Great on the Tigris, joined by a bridge to old Nineveh, which lies waste, though the streets and palaces can still be traced in the ruin. Seven thousand Jews, and at their head R. Zakkai the Nasi of the line of David and R. Joseph called Burhan-al-Mulk, astronomer to Sayf al-Din, brother of the king of Damascus. The synagogue of Obadiah stands here, and that of Jonah son of Amittai, and that of Nahum the Elkoshite. Benjamin is inside the country the Head of the Captivity's writ runs over.
suggested_refs: Mosul and the ruins of Nineveh; the prophetic tomb-synagogues Benjamin lists there
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Amadia, the memory of David Alroy
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The Alroy rising itself is placed around 1160, a decade before Benjamin's passage; he reports it as recent history, not as something seen.
stops.campa: In the mountains of Kurdistan, twenty-five thousand Jews in a hundred communities, speaking the language of the Targum, and the memory ten years old of Menahem son of Solomon, whom they called David Alroy. He told the Jews of the mountains he was the messiah, and that he would take Jerusalem out of the hands of the Gentiles, and men came to him with weapons in their hands. He was killed in his own bed. Benjamin writes the episode down in full, and because he does, it is the only account of it history has.
suggested_refs: The rising of David Alroy in Kurdistan, known to history solely through this passage
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Alroy'

stops.name: Baghdad, forty thousand and ten academies
stops.date_confidence: Contested. The pool's chronology lens dates Baghdad 1168, its quotes lens c. 1170. The count itself is a manuscript decision: Adler's n. 127 gives 40,000 in the British Museum and Casanatense manuscripts against 1,000 in Asher and the printed editions.
stops.campa: Three miles of city along the Tigris, and the caliph, whom Benjamin calls the Emir al Muminin al Abbasi, sits in a palace with a park and a lake and wild beasts inside its wall. He reads and writes the holy language, he knows the law of Israel, and he comes out once in the year, at the feast the Mohammedans call El-id-bed Ramazan. Three centuries before, Ziryab left this city for Cordoba and built a court there out of what he carried in his head. Benjamin has come the other way, west to east, and this is the far end of his road.
stops.quote: In Bagdad there are about 40,000 Jews, and they dwell in security, prosperity and honour under the great Caliph, and amongst them are great sages, the heads of Academies engaged in the study of the law. In this city there are ten Academies.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on Baghdad
suggested_refs: Adler's footnote 123 identifying the caliph as al-Mustanjid (r. 1160-1170), not al-Mustadi; footnote 127 on the 40,000 / 1,000 manuscript split
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h, nn. 123 and 127
ziryab.journey.json

stops.name: Baghdad, the Head of the Captivity
stops.date_confidence: Same visit as the preceding stop, split for what it records; the day is a placement.
stops.campa: Daniel son of Hisdai, Head of the Captivity of all Israel, holds a pedigree back to David and a firman from the caliph, and every fifth day he goes up to the palace with horsemen of Israel and Gentiles both, and criers going before him calling out to make way for the son of David. He is seated opposite the caliph, in fulfilment of the verse that the sceptre shall not depart from Judah. His authority runs from Persia to Yemen, from Mesopotamia to the mountains of Ararat and the land of the Alans.
stops.quote: He is mounted on a horse, and is attired in robes of silk and embroidery with a large turban on his head, and from the turban is suspended a long white cloth adorned with a chain upon which the cipher of Mohammed is engraved.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on the Exilarch at Baghdad
suggested_refs: The office of the Exilarch under the Abbasid caliphate, and the Genesis 49:10 protocol Benjamin reports at the audience
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Baghdad, the Academy Gaon Jacob
stops.date_confidence: Same visit, split for what it records. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from ibn_battuta.journey.json.
stops.campa: Ten academies in one city, and the men who run them are named one after another as though Benjamin were reading a list off a wall: R. Hananiah, Warden of the Levites; R. Daniel; R. Elazar the Scholar; R. Elazar son of Zemach, who keeps the genealogy of Samuel the Prophet. Twenty-eight synagogues, some in the city and some across the river. A hundred and sixty years later Ibn Battuta will reach this same bank and find Baghdad sacked, emptied by the Mongols, the academies gone out of it.
stops.quote: At the head of the great Academy is the chief rabbi R. Samuel, the son of Eli. He is the head of the Academy Gaon Jacob. He is a Levite, and traces his pedigree back to Moses our teacher.
stops.quote_source: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), on the academies of Baghdad
suggested_refs: The ten Baghdad academies and twenty-eight synagogues enumerated in the Itinerary
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
ibn_battuta.journey.json

stops.name: Al-Kifl, the tomb of Ezekiel
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The identification of the shrine with Al-Kifl is a later siting, not fixed by Benjamin, who gives only a day's distance from Baghdad.
stops.campa: A day out from Baghdad, on the Euphrates, the synagogue of Ezekiel the priest stands in front of the prophet's grave with sixty towers around it, and between every pair of towers another synagogue, and in the court the ark, and behind it the tomb, and a lamp burning above it that has not gone out since the day he was buried. Jews come here from Persia and Media at the New Year and on the Day of Atonement. The library the prophet is said to have gathered is kept in the vault, with books from the first Temple and the second.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Ezekiel and its perpetual lamp; siting at Al-Kifl per Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Kifl, Al-'
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Kifl, Al-' and 'Ezekiel's Tomb'

stops.name: Susa, the coffin hung from the bridge
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. The Sanjar settlement Benjamin recounts is itself older than his visit and reaches him as local report.
stops.campa: Shushan the capital, and the river running through the middle of it, and on the one bank the Jews are rich and keep synagogues, and on the other bank they are poor, because the coffin of Daniel lies on the rich side and the traffic follows the bones. The two banks fight over it for years, until Sanjar Shah ben Shah orders the coffin taken up and hung in a case of polished glass from the middle of the bridge, over open water, so that neither side holds it and both may look at it. The case is still hanging over the water when Benjamin comes down the road to see it.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Daniel at Susa and Sanjar's adjudication by suspension over the river
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Ispahan, where the eyewitness ends
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed, and the last stop that may be first-hand. Adler's footnote 122 holds that the figures beyond Hadara look exaggerated and lend colour to the view that Benjamin did not proceed beyond Ispahan, the intervening places resting on hearsay.
stops.campa: Ispahan, the great city and the royal residence, twelve miles round, fifteen thousand Jews, and R. Sallah at their head, appointed by the Head of the Captivity to rule all the rabbis in the kingdom of Persia. Past this point the numbers swell and the roads lengthen, and Adler's own note concedes the likelihood that Benjamin went no further himself. What follows is what merchants told him: Shiraz, Ghazna, the Ghuz who eat no bread and drink no wine but feed on uncooked meat, and the rout of Sanjar in the mountains.
suggested_refs: Adler's footnote 122, the scholarly boundary between Benjamin's eyewitness account and his hearsay
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h, n. 122
EBSCO Research Starters, 'Benjamin of Tudela'

stops.name: Kish, the emporium in the Gulf
stops.date_confidence: Reported rather than certainly walked; whether Benjamin reached the Gulf himself or turned south from Iraq is disputed and left open here.
stops.campa: An island in the sea, six miles across, with no field and no garden on it and one spring; the people live entirely by trade. Men of India and the islands bring silk and cotton and hemp, wheat and barley and millet and rice, and the men of Shinar and Yemen and Persia bring the goods of the west, and the two meet here and change hands, and four hundred Jews live in the middle of it. This is the emporium of Benjamin's east, and he names it exactly, without any of the marvels that fill the pages around it.
suggested_refs: Kish Island as the twelfth-century Gulf entrepot between India and Mesopotamia
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Aden, the Jews who hold the mountains
stops.date_confidence: Reported. The text runs Zebid, then Aden, then twenty days to Assuan, but the eastward and southern legs cannot be separated into travelled and reported with confidence.
stops.campa: In the mountains above Aden the Jews are not under the yoke of the Gentiles. They hold cities and castles on the summits, and they come down into the plain country of Aden, which is Eden in Telassar, and take spoil and booty and go back up, and no man can prevail against them. Many of them travel as far as Egypt and Persia to trade. Everywhere else on the road a community holds what a king allows it to hold. Here the holding is the mountain itself, and Benjamin names no charter and no protector.
suggested_refs: The independent mountain Jews of the Yemeni highlands as the Itinerary describes them
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Mecca, the House reported at second hand
stops.date_confidence: Not a visit. Benjamin never reaches Mecca and reports the Arabian interior from merchants. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from ibn_battuta.journey.json and carries a gap, not a stop.
stops.campa: Benjamin never goes to Mecca. He is told about the Arabian interior by men who have, and he writes down what they say: the desert of Saba, the tribes that keep the law of Israel, the pilgrim road. The report is pinned to the House itself, at the sanctuary's own coordinate, though Benjamin's own feet never cross it. The pin marks the place where the eyes stop and the ears begin. Everything south and east of Ispahan arrives in the book by this route.
suggested_refs: The Arabian sections of the Itinerary, flagged by Adler and by later scholarship as secondhand
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

segments.name: The Return, and the Book After Him

stops.name: Alexandria, the Pharos and the twenty academies
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the 1173 colophon working backward; Adler's bracket for the absence from Europe closes in 1171.
stops.campa: The city Alexander built, laid out in streets so straight a man can see from one gate to the other, and outside the walls the foundations of twenty academies with a marble column standing between each, where Aristotle taught. On the sea stands the Pharos, and in its top a mirror of glass in which a watchman can see a ship fifty days out. Three thousand Jews live in the city, and merchants of every nation trade in it, from Andalusia and Provence to Yemen and India. Benjamin counts the nations as carefully as the Jews.
suggested_refs: The Pharos and its reported mirror; Benjamin's roster of the trading nations of Alexandria
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Fustat, the head of all the congregations
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Adler's footnote 2 records that Benjamin found the Fatimid caliph still the acknowledged ruler; the Itinerary contains no allusion to the deposition of 10 September 1171 and never names Saladin. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from maimonides.journey.json.
stops.campa: Mizraim on the Nile, the old city, two thousand Jews, and two synagogues that read the Torah on different cycles, the men of the land of Israel finishing in one year and the men of Babylon in three, and they come together to pray on the festivals. At their head is Nethanel, Prince of Princes and head of the Academy, who appoints the rabbis and the officials of all Egypt. Moses Maimonides has been living in this quarter since 1166 and leading this community. Neither man's writing records a meeting.
suggested_refs: The Palestinian and Babylonian congregations of Fustat and their divergent Torah cycles; Adler's footnote 2 on Fatimid Egypt
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h, n. 2 and preface
maimonides.journey.json

stops.name: Palermo, the palace of King William
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the 1173 colophon; the return leg carries no dates at all in the text.
stops.campa: Fifteen hundred Jews in Palermo, and the palace of King William standing in a garden with a fountain fed by water led underground, walled about, and a lake in the park with vessels of silver and gold upon it, where the king takes his pleasure with the women of his household. Two hundred Jews at Messina, where the strait runs so hard that ships are lost in it. Benjamin has crossed back into Latin Christendom, and Palermo gets what Aleppo got: a count, a king's house, a distance to the next town.
suggested_refs: The Norman palace and park of William II at Palermo; note the return route runs Sicily, Rome, Lucca, the Alpine passes, Verdun, and the Rhineland
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h

stops.name: Castile, the book brought home
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested in the colophon (4933 / 1173); the place is not. The text names the country, not a town, so this pin is a placement inside Castile and nothing more.
stops.campa: He brought this book with him on his return to the country of Castile, in the year 4933. That is the whole of the ending: no town named, no house, no welcome, no death. The road home has run from Sicily to Rome, up through Lucca and the mountain of Jean de Maurienne, over the passes of Italy to Verdun, and along the Rhineland communities of Alamannia, the congregations Bernard of Clairvaux rode into Mainz to save from a crusading mob in 1146, before turning south again. Nothing after 1173 is recorded of him anywhere. No source gives the year he died, and no grave has ever been claimed.
suggested_refs: The colophon of the Sefer ha-Masa'ot, the only statement of the journey's end
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h, colophon
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Benjamin of Tudela'

stops.name: Constantinople, the first printing
stops.date_confidence: Attested year; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Three hundred and seventy years after he brings the book home, Eliezer ben Gershon sets the Hebrew of the Sefer ha-Masa'ot in rabbinic type at Constantinople, sixty-four pages in octavo, in the city whose fence between Rabbanites and Karaites Benjamin had measured with his own eyes. Ferrara follows in 1556 from the press of Abraham ben Usque, with fewer scribal errors, and after it Freiburg, Leiden, Amsterdam, Altdorf, Sulzbach, Zolkiev, Lemberg and Warsaw, and the Latin of Arias Montano at Antwerp.
suggested_refs: The 1543 Constantinople editio princeps; note the 1556 Ferrara edition is not Benjamin Musafia's, an anachronism of half a century
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Benjamin of Tudela'
Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Introduction

stops.name: Oxford, the critical text
stops.date_confidence: Attested year of publication; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Marcus Nathan Adler prints the critical text from a manuscript in the British Museum, with the Hebrew, an English translation and the commentary that settles what Benjamin can and cannot be made to say. It is the footnotes that hold the numbers apart: forty thousand Jews at Baghdad in the British Museum and Casanatense manuscripts against one thousand in Asher and the printed editions, the caliph identified as al-Mustanjid, the road beyond Ispahan marked hearsay. Every later reader works from this book.
suggested_refs: M. N. Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela: Critical Text, Translation and Commentary (Oxford University Press, 1907); L. Grunhut's competing Jerusalem edition of 1902 was not consulted
sources: Adler, The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (1907), Project Gutenberg 14981-h
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Benjamin of Tudela'

stops.name: Tudela, the bronze in the Plaza de la Juderia
stops.date_confidence: 1994 per English and Spanish Wikipedia and the Navarre heritage sources. A 1984 date circulates but belongs to a separate monument to the Sephardic community; the bust's own inscription was not recovered, so this rests on secondary agreement.
stops.campa: Ricardo Varela Andres casts a head in bronze and sets it in the Plaza de la Juderia, in the quarter of the town Benjamin left, and it is invented out of nothing, because no portrait, seal or image of him survives or has ever been claimed to survive. Streets carry the name here, in Rehavia in Jerusalem, and in Tel Aviv, and a secondary school in Tudela carries it too. The man who spent eight years writing down other people's names has a bust with no face behind it and a book with no author inside it.
suggested_refs: The Varela Andres bust in the Plaza de la Juderia, Tudela; the absence of any medieval iconographic model for it
sources: Wikipedia, 'Benjamin of Tudela'
Universidad de Navarra, Catedra de Patrimonio y Arte Navarro, 'Un paseo por la escultura conmemorativa de Tudela'
